The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. Arthur Conan Doyle's 1892 collection of twelve short stories features detective Sherlock Holmes and his companion Dr. Watson, showcasing the detective's methods, personality, and range of cases. The stories popularized the detective archetype and established many of the techniques and mannerisms that define investigative fiction.

Published as a collection after Holmes appeared in earlier serialized stories, these tales solidified the character's fame and legacy. The stories feature various cases—a scandal in Bohemia, a case of identity, a red-headed league, a twisted lip—each demonstrating Holmes's deductive methods. Holmes employs techniques ahead of his time: observation of minute details, logical deduction, forensic evidence, and psychological insight into criminal behavior.

Watson narrates most stories, providing both grounding and a perspective through which readers understand Holmes's seemingly magical abilities. The collection establishes Holmes's quirks and habits: his violin playing, his indifference to social convention, his reliance on tobacco and cocaine. The stories introduce the concept of deduction as entertainment—the pleasure of watching an impossible mystery resolved through reason. A Scandal in Bohemia features Irene Adler, the one woman Holmes respects and admires, establishing the detective's rare vulnerability. These early stories made Holmes a cultural phenomenon and remain foundational to the detective fiction genre.
